summary: An informational memo extending network address translators to share load, so sessions can be spread across a pool of servers rather than sent to one server.

plainLanguage.summary: A front desk that sends visitors to different workers so one is not overwhelmed.

questions: how does load sharing nat work
how can nat balance server load
what are limitations of load sharing nat
subtitle: Using network address translation to spread server load across a pool of machines.

tldr.problem: A single server can become overwhelmed when many clients try to connect to it at once. Traditional load balancers require special hardware or client changes, making them expensive and complex.
tldr.mechanism: LSNAT (Load Share NAT) is a router that sits between clients and a pool of identical servers. When a client connects to a virtual server address, the router transparently redirects the connection to one of the real servers based on a load-sharing algorithm, without the client or servers knowing.
tldr.outcome: Servers can be seamlessly added to the pool, load is automatically balanced among them, and clients need no changes—the load balancing is invisible to both client and server applications.

today: RFC 2391 is an Informational RFC from August 1998 describing a transparent load-balancing approach using NAT. While LSNAT as described here was not widely deployed, the concepts influenced later load-balancing technologies. Modern load balancers (hardware and software) operate on similar principles but with more sophisticated session affinity, real-time health checking, and integration with application layers. Cloud providers use variants of these concepts for distributing traffic across server pools.

sections.title: Introduction to Load Sharing NAT
sections.content:
Network Address Translation (NAT), defined in RFC 1631, traditionally allows private networks to connect to the public internet using only a few public IP addresses. RFC 2391 extends this idea with LSNAT (Load Share NAT), which uses address translation to distribute incoming client sessions across a pool of servers.

Unlike traditional NATs that translate addresses only for outbound traffic from private networks, LSNATs translate inbound traffic, taking incoming connections meant for a single virtual server address and spreading them across multiple physical servers. This happens transparently: the clients and servers see ordinary address translation and have no idea their session was selected based on current server load.

The RFC emphasizes two advantages. First, no changes are needed to clients or server software—the load sharing happens at the network layer. Second, the load distribution can be customized to specific services or tuned to account for server capabilities. The traditional approach of having DNS servers shuffle the order of resource records works poorly because DNS changes propagate slowly and do not reflect real-time load variations.

This document covers how LSNATs work in different network topologies: in a globally unique address space, alongside traditional NAT for private networks, and in configurations without topological constraints on server placement.
sections.plainLanguage: A load-sharing translator takes messages meant for one address and routes them to different servers based on how busy each one is. Clients think they are talking to one server, but they are actually spread across many.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines several important terms. A session is a complete conversation between a client and server, initiated with the first packet and terminated when both sides disconnect. The start of session is when translation parameters are established: for TCP, this is when the SYN bit is set without the ACK bit; for UDP and other protocols, there is no deterministic way to know, so LSNATs use heuristics. The end of session is when a TCP connection closes (detected by FIN or RST flags) or, for other protocols, when a timeout occurs (e.g., after 1 minute of inactivity).

Session flow refers to the direction the session was initiated (inbound or outbound), different from packet flow, which is just which direction a particular packet went. This distinction matters because a single session involves packets in both directions.

The RFC also explains the distinction between LSNAT and traditional NAT. Traditional NATs bind a private address to a public address and apply that binding to all sessions from that private host. LSNATs, instead, bind each incoming session (identified by a tuple of source address, source port, destination address, and destination port) to a selected server, independent of other sessions from the same client. This allows load balancing even for sessions from the same client.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is like a phone conversation: it starts with the first ring, continues while you talk, and ends when someone hangs up. The LSNAT watches the start of each new conversation and sends it to a different worker based on who is least busy.

sections.title: How LSNAT Routes and Translates
sections.content:
When a client sends the first packet of a new session to the virtual server address, the LSNAT router performs session binding: it examines the current load on each server in the pool (using metrics like number of active sessions, traffic volume, or response time) and selects one server. The address translation parameters for that session are then recorded.

All subsequent packets in that session are subject to address lookup and translation. For inbound packets (from client to server), the LSNAT translates the destination IP address from the virtual server address to the selected real server's address, and also translates the destination port if needed. The TCP/UDP checksum and IP header checksum are recalculated. For outbound packets (from server to client), the source address is translated back to the virtual server address.

The RFC describes three operational scenarios. In the first, all servers have globally unique addresses in the same address space as clients, and the LSNAT sits on the border router between them. In the second, LSNAT works alongside traditional NAT, with the LSNAT handling inbound load balancing and NAT handling outbound address translation for a private server network. In the third, the virtual server address is the same as the LSNAT router's own interface address, a configuration called LS-NAPT (Load Share NAPT). This approach removes topological constraints because all packets are forced to traverse the router, but it requires more complex translation and limits concurrent sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: When a client calls the virtual server, the LSNAT switchboard looks at how busy each real server is and routes the call there. All calls in that conversation keep going to the same server, so the session does not get split up.

sections.title: Load Sharing Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC describes several algorithms for selecting which server to use. The simplest is round-robin: just cycle through the servers in order, regardless of their actual load. This is easy to implement but treats all sessions as equal, even though a file transfer (FTP) uses more resources than a quick telnet command.

Least-load-first improves on round-robin by selecting the server with the fewest active sessions. Least-traffic-first goes further, measuring server load by the number of bytes or packets sent to or from each server over time, which is a better proxy for resource consumption. Least-weighted-load allows administrators to assign weights to both session types (FTP might be 5x the weight of telnet) and to servers themselves (a faster server might have a higher weight), so the algorithm can account for heterogeneous capabilities.

The RFC also mentions response-time-based selection: periodically ping each server and use the response time as a metric of how busy it is. This requires active probing but gives more accurate real-time information about server state.

The memo does not mandate any particular algorithm; different deployments can choose based on their needs. All algorithms share the property that once a session is bound to a server, it stays with that server for its entire lifetime—no mid-session switching to a different server.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can pick which server in many ways: take turns (round-robin), pick the one with the fewest customers (least-load), measure how much data is flowing to each (least-traffic), or ask each how busy it is (response-time).

sections.title: Limitations and Constraints
sections.content:
LSNAT has several important limitations. Most critically, all requests and responses for a session must traverse the same LSNAT router. This means the router must be on the only path between clients and servers. For this reason, the RFC recommends placing the LSNAT on a single border router to the stub domain containing the servers. If traffic could bypass the router and go directly to a server, the server would send its reply directly back to the client without the router's address translation, breaking the session.

Second, LSNAT cannot switch a session to a different server mid-stream. Once a session is assigned to a server, it stays there until the session ends, even if that server becomes much busier than others. This is because LSNAT tracks load by session, not by packet-by-packet responsiveness.

Third, LSNAT is limited to TCP, UDP, and ICMP query protocols. Other transport protocols (like SCTP or GRE) cannot be load-balanced by LSNAT because there is no way to identify sessions.

Fourth, like traditional NAT, LSNAT breaks the end-to-end semantics of IP addresses. Applications that embed IP addresses in their data (like FTP passive mode) may not work correctly. The RFC also inherits all limitations of NAT from RFC 1631.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest catch is that everything has to go through the same router, so it only works on the edge of a network. Also, once a customer is assigned to a worker, they stay there even if another worker becomes free. And it only works for the most common types of network conversations.
